## Problem formulation {.section-break #optimistic-problem data-section="3 · Problem formulation"}

<div class="section-number">3</div>
<div class="section-subtitle">Disturbance-aware monitoring with optimism over plausible executions.</div>
<div class="section-agenda">Current information, policy decision, constraints and monitoring cost</div>

## The decision at one replanning time {#optimistic-decision data-section="3 · Problem formulation"}

At physical time $t_k$, the robot knows its state $x_k$, clarity vector $q_k$, disturbance belief $\mathcal B_k^d$, environment geometry and target clarity $\bar q$.

Choose a **nominal policy parameter vector** $\theta\in\Theta$:

$$u_{\mathrm{nom}}(\tau)=\pi^{\mathrm{nom}}(\tau,x(\tau),q(\tau);\mathcal B_k^d,\theta),\qquad 0\leq\tau\leq T.$$

<div class="definition-grid"><div>$k$: physical replanning index.<br>$\Theta$: bounded policy parameter domain.<br>$\theta$: one vector that specifies a nominal policy.</div><div>$T$: prediction horizon.<br>$\tau$: elapsed prediction time.<br>$u_{\mathrm{nom}}$: control input requested by that policy.</div></div>

The execution filter determines the applied input $u$. Its resulting motion determines sensing and clarity.

<div class="key-line">One sampled parameter vector specifies one policy to evaluate. A trajectory is an output of that evaluation.</div>

::: {.notes}
Updated source: Paper Pitch Development, pp. 2–5 and 7. A policy can be represented by a reference trajectory and a tracking controller, but the generic method does not choose a particular vehicle model or parameter count. Theta dependence is suppressed on state and clarity for readability. The nominal policy and the design policy used to construct the filter are different objects. The design policy was introduced in the preliminaries.
:::

## Monitoring cost and admissible motion {#optimistic-task data-section="3 · Problem formulation"}

For a possible spatial disturbance field $d$, predict the executed state and clarity:

$$\dot x=f_d(x,u,d(\Psi(x))),\qquad
\dot q_j=\frac{C_j(x)^2}{R}(1-q_j)^2-Q_jq_j^2.$$

$$x(0)=x_k,\quad q(0)=q_k,\quad u(\tau)\in\mathcal U,\quad h_a(x(\tau))\leq0\quad\forall a.$$

<div class="definition-grid"><div>$\Psi(x)$: position extracted from state.<br>$h_a$: state or environment constraint indexed by $a$; positive values indicate violation.</div><div>$\mathcal U$: admissible actuator inputs.<br>$C_j,R,Q_j$: sensing quality, measurement noise and monitored-process noise, as defined in the preliminaries.</div></div>

$$J(\theta;d)=\int_0^T q_d(q(\tau))\,d\tau,\qquad
q_d(q)=\frac1{N_p}\sum_{j=1}^{N_p}[\bar q_j-q_j]_+.$$

<div class="key-line">Lower cost means less accumulated monitoring deficit along the predicted executed motion.</div>
<div class="small-note">The method checks finitely many disturbance fields and numerical trajectory points. Those checks do not certify all possible executions.</div>

## Expected performance and optimistic performance {#optimistic-two-criteria data-section="3 · Problem formulation"}

**Disturbance-aware expected-cost criterion:** choose a policy with low average monitoring cost under the current disturbance belief.

**Proposed optimistic criterion:** choose a policy with low monitoring cost among a specified fraction of its favorable plausible executions.

Both criteria use the same disturbed dynamics, execution filter, sensing model and motion checks.

$$\boxed{\mathcal B^d(\tau)=\mathcal B_k^d\qquad 0\leq\tau\leq T}$$

<div class="two-points"><div><b>Inside prediction</b><br>The posterior remains fixed. The controller still responds to every predicted state.</div><div><b>After real execution</b><br>Actual observations update POAM. The next planning call uses that updated posterior.</div></div>

<div class="key-line">Optimism can favor trying an uncertain alternative. A later monitoring benefit remains an experimental hypothesis.</div>

::: {.notes}
Source: Paper Pitch Development, pp. 5–6 and 10–12. This revision does not simulate hypothetical observations or posterior reductions. It therefore does not compute the value of learning. Favorable-tail cost is a decision criterion, not an estimate of expected monitoring cost. The explicit empirical definition follows after the execution model.
:::

## Method {.section-break #optimistic-method data-section="4 · Proposed method"}

<div class="section-number">4</div>
<div class="section-subtitle">Predict executed monitoring, score favorable outcomes, then refine policy parameters.</div>
<div class="section-agenda">Execution prediction, optimistic objective, adapted MBD proposal and real learning</div>

## Architecture of the proposed method {#optimistic-architecture data-section="4 · Method architecture"}

<img class="architecture architecture-main" src="assets/optimistic_architecture.svg" alt="Current state, clarity and wind belief enter MBD. Its policy samples are evaluated through disturbed filtered motion and clarity. Optimistic costs and feasibility guide refinement. After optimization, fresh-field reevaluation selects a policy; real execution and observations update the next planning input." />

::: {.notes}
Method design for review. The diagram separates the numerical search loop from the physical execution loop. Only the latter changes the disturbance posterior. The optimistic score affects the target density and final selection. The mixture proposal changes search efficiency and is corrected by importance weights. No revised simulation result is presented.
:::

## Two sets of disturbance fields serve different purposes {#two-field-banks data-section="4 · Executed monitoring prediction"}

Let $\mathcal P_k^d$ be the spatial-field distribution represented by the current POAM belief $\mathcal B_k^d$.

| Field set | How it is obtained | What it evaluates |
|---|---|---|
| **Performance fields** $d^{[s]}$, $s=1,\ldots,S$ | Draw from $\mathcal P_k^d$ | One complete monitoring cost per field |
| **Construction fields** $\widetilde d^{[\ell]}$, $\ell=1,\ldots,L$ | Use the execution filter's sampling rule | Largest constraint value in design-policy rollouts |

Each realization is a coherent spatial function. Its value changes with position, and it remains the same field throughout a rollout.

<div class="key-line">Optimism acts on monitoring costs. The filter retains its adverse construction samples.</div>
<div class="small-note">Fix these fields or their base random draws within one planning call. Recompute trajectories and constraint values at each queried state.</div>

::: {.notes}
Source: Paper Pitch Development, pp. 2–4. Performance fields must be posterior-probability samples. The source RPCBF paper uses informed sampling including uniform bounded samples and vertices; those are not probability samples for a monitoring-cost average. A posterior-informed construction bank is an adaptation whose rule must match the runtime filter. Do not independently redraw a wind vector at every integration step or remove unfavorable construction samples after seeing optimistic costs.
:::

## Nominal and design policies have different roles {#two-policy-roles data-section="4 · Executed monitoring prediction"}

| Policy | Role | Chosen by MBD? |
|---|---|---|
| $\pi^{\mathrm{nom}}(\tau,x,q;\mathcal B_k^d,\theta)$ | Requests the inputs that pursue monitoring | Yes, through $\theta$ |
| $\pi_D(x;\mathcal B_k^d)$ | Supplies a specified continuation for evaluating future constraint values | No |

**Example:** the nominal policy requests motion toward an inspection region. The design policy predicts braking from the current position and velocity under the tested disturbances.

A predicted braking violation can require the execution filter to change the nominal request.

<div class="key-line">The design-policy rollout constructs a constraint test. It is separate from the monitoring rollout being scored.</div>
<div class="source">RPCBF-inspired construction. The generic method retains the chosen design policy and nominal-policy representation.</div>

## Construct a constraint value at the queried state {#state-dependent-value data-section="4 · Executed monitoring prediction"}

For each construction field, start at the currently queried state $x$ and follow the design policy:

$$\dot z^{[\ell]}=f_d\!\left(z^{[\ell]},\pi_D(z^{[\ell]};\mathcal B_k^d),
\widetilde d^{[\ell]}(\Psi(z^{[\ell]}))\right),\qquad z^{[\ell]}(0)=x.$$

Fit a cubic spline $s_{a\ell}(\sigma;x)$ through the values of $h_a(z^{[\ell]}(\sigma))$. Compute

$$V_{a,k}(x)=\max_{\ell=1,\ldots,L}\ \max_{0\leq\sigma\leq T_B}s_{a\ell}(\sigma;x),
\qquad \nabla_xV_{a,k}(x).$$

<div class="definition-grid"><div>$z^{[\ell]}$: design-policy trajectory.<br>$T_B$: design-policy evaluation horizon.<br>$\sigma$: time within that short rollout.</div><div>$s_{a\ell}$: interpolated constraint value.<br>$V_{a,k}$: largest tested value.<br>$\nabla_xV_{a,k}$: state sensitivity.</div></div>

<div class="key-line">Maximize the spline over time, including interior extrema. A maximum over integration nodes alone is a different approximation.</div>
<div class="source">Adapted from Knoedler et al., Algorithm 1 and Eqs. (18)–(21). A closed finite interval includes its endpoint in this presentation.</div>

::: {.notes}
The design policy is fixed during this construction. The fields remain fixed spatial functions, but differentiation includes their dependence on the queried position along z. Holding a recorded sequence of wind vectors constant while differentiating the path would drop that dependence. At ties the maximum can be nondifferentiable; numerical derivative conventions and regularity require explicit treatment during implementation. The PDF writes 0<=sigma<T_B; we include the terminal point as an explicit finite-horizon checking convention.
:::

## Compute the applied input at that state {#state-dependent-filter data-section="4 · Executed monitoring prediction"}

For control-affine disturbed dynamics, write

$$f_d(x,u,\delta)=f_0(x,\delta)+G(x,\delta)u,\qquad
\delta_\ell(x)=\widetilde d^{[\ell]}(\Psi(x)).$$

With a polyhedral actuator set $\mathcal U$, the execution filter solves the **quadratic program (QP)**

$$\begin{aligned}
u=\Gamma_k(x,u_{\mathrm{nom}})
&\in\underset{v\in\mathcal U}{\arg\min}\ \tfrac12\|v-u_{\mathrm{nom}}\|_2^2\\
\text{subject to }\quad
\nabla_xV_{a,k}(x)^{\mathsf T}[f_0(x,\delta_\ell)+G(x,\delta_\ell)v]
&\leq-\kappa V_{a,k}(x),\quad \forall a,\ell.
\end{aligned}$$

<div class="definition-grid"><div>$f_0$: uncontrolled drift; $G$: input matrix.<br>$\delta_\ell$: tested disturbance at this state.<br>$v$: trial input; $\Gamma_k$: resulting input map.</div><div>$\kappa>0$: value-rate coefficient.<br>One input must satisfy all listed inequalities.<br>A feasible nominal input remains unchanged.</div></div>

<div class="small-note">This is our explicit finite-sample formulation inspired by RPCBF, using a linear value-rate function. It is not a verbatim expansion of the paper's Eq. (19) or a general safety certificate.</div>

::: {.notes}
Source: Paper Pitch Development, p. 4. The source paper's Eq. (19) has a supremum-over-disturbance then infimum-over-input ordering. We explicitly require a common input for all sampled inequalities and do not claim that this stronger finite-sample formulation follows merely by interchanging those extrema. A polyhedral actuator set makes the displayed control-affine formulation a QP; a general convex actuator set instead yields a convex optimization problem with a quadratic objective. Numerical gradients, sample coverage and finite prediction limit guarantees. Planning and execution must use the same filter and prescribed infeasibility response.
:::

## A fixed belief still gives a changing controller {#fixed-belief-changing-control data-section="4 · Executed monitoring prediction"}

Each performance realization has its own reached state. At every predicted control step:

1. Evaluate the nominal policy at that reached state.
2. Rebuild the design-policy trajectories, spline maxima and state gradients.
3. Solve the QP at that state, then propagate motion in that performance field.
4. Update clarity from the resulting position.

$$\begin{aligned}
u_{\mathrm{nom}}^{[s]}&=\pi^{\mathrm{nom}}(\tau,x^{[s]},q^{[s]};\mathcal B_k^d,\theta),\\
u^{[s]}&=\Gamma_k(x^{[s]},u_{\mathrm{nom}}^{[s]}),\\
\dot x^{[s]}&=f_d(x^{[s]},u^{[s]},d^{[s]}(\Psi(x^{[s]}))).
\end{aligned}$$

<div class="key-line">Different wind fields can produce different states and interventions even though the posterior is fixed.</div>
<div class="small-note">The hidden performance field enters the simulated physical dynamics. It is not supplied as known wind to the nominal policy or filter.</div>

## Each performance field gives one monitoring cost {#performance-costs data-section="4 · Optimistic monitoring objective"}

For the same policy parameters $\theta$, every performance prediction starts from $x_k,q_k$ and accumulates clarity deficit:

$$J_s(\theta)=\int_0^Tq_d(q^{[s]}(\tau))\,d\tau,\qquad
\widehat J_k(\theta)=\frac1S\sum_{s=1}^{S}J_s(\theta).$$

<div class="definition-grid"><div>$J_s$: cost in performance field $s$.<br>$q^{[s]}$: clarity along that field's executed trajectory.</div><div>$\widehat J_k$: sampled expected cost.<br>$S$: number of performance fields.</div></div>

The nominal route can be short while the predicted execution is slow, deflected, or repeatedly interrupted by the filter. Those effects change sensing and therefore $J_s$.

<div class="key-line">The cost already includes travel and monitoring consequences. No separate wind-variance or filter-intervention reward is added.</div>

## Optimism selects a favorable fraction of costs {#optimistic-tail-cost data-section="4 · Optimistic monitoring objective"}

Sort the $S$ costs for one policy: $J_{(1)}(\theta)\leq\cdots\leq J_{(S)}(\theta)$.
Choose a fraction $\eta\in(0,1]$ and define $m=\lfloor\eta S\rfloor$, $r=\eta S-m$.

$$\boxed{J^{\mathrm{opt}}_{k,\eta}(\theta)=
\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{s=1}^{m}J_{(s)}(\theta)+rJ_{(m+1)}(\theta)}{\eta S}}$$

<div class="definition-grid"><div>$\eta$: fraction of favorable outcomes retained.<br>$m$: number of fully included sorted costs.<br>$r\in[0,1)$: fractional weight on the next cost.</div><div>Omit the fractional term when $r=0$.<br>$\eta=1$: recover the expected cost.<br>$\eta S<1$: use the minimum sampled cost.</div></div>

<div class="key-line">Smaller $\eta$ expresses more optimism about monitoring performance.</div>
<div class="small-note">Known strong wind remains in the model. If all fields give the same cost, optimism does not change that cost.</div>

::: {.notes}
Source: Paper Pitch Development, pp. 5–6. This is the empirical lower partial mean for costs, also describable as a favorable lower-tail average. It is not upper-tail risk-averse CVaR and is not the expected value of information. m=0 is valid, with an empty sum. At eta=1, m=S and r=0, so J_(S+1) must not be evaluated. Two fields and eta=0.25 reduce to a single minimum, which is a poorly resolved tail criterion. Sample count and eta need separate sensitivity studies.
:::

## Example: an uncertain policy can become preferable {#optimism-cost-example data-section="4 · Optimistic monitoring objective"}

**Illustrative costs only.** Four equally weighted performance fields, with all policies passing the motion checks. Lower is better.

| Policy | Sorted costs | Expected cost | Optimistic cost, $\eta=0.5$ |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| Established route | $9,10,10,11$ | **10** | 9.5 |
| Uncertain alternative | $6,8,14,20$ | 12 | **7** |
| Poor alternative | $11,13,16,20$ | 15 | 12 |
| Known costly route | $12,12,12,12$ | 12 | 12 |

The uncertain alternative loses on average and wins under the favorable-half criterion. The poor alternative remains unattractive even in its favorable outcomes.

<div class="key-line">This preference is deliberate optimism. The table does not demonstrate a later learning benefit.</div>

::: {.notes}
All numbers are invented explicitly for arithmetic teaching and are not performance measurements. For eta=0.625 the uncertain alternative has eta*S=2.5 and score (6+8+0.5*14)/2.5=8.4. The interactive walkthrough below uses eta=0.5 to illustrate the sequence of calculations.
:::

## Numerical acceptance applies to every tested field {#optimistic-acceptance data-section="4 · Optimistic monitoring objective"}

Let $v_k(\theta)=1$ only when the policy passes all declared numerical checks in every performance rollout:

- Finite state propagation and monitoring cost.
- No detected state-constraint violation.
- Successful QP execution without an infeasibility fallback.

Otherwise $v_k(\theta)=0$ and the policy receives zero MBD weight.

$$v_k(\theta)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\text{reject the policy, regardless of its favorable costs}.$$

<div class="key-line">The lower tail changes cost preference. It never hides a failed unfavorable realization.</div>
<div class="small-note">Planning must reproduce the actual filter and fallback behavior. A finite sampled acceptance test does not establish continuous-time or all-disturbance safety.</div>

## The optimistic target density {#optimistic-target data-section="4 · MBD optimization"}

MBD's clean optimization variable is the nominal parameter vector: $y_0=\theta$.

$$p_{0,k}(\theta)=\frac1{Z_k}\,\mathbf1_\Theta(\theta)\,v_k(\theta)
\exp\!\left(-\frac{J^{\mathrm{opt}}_{k,\eta}(\theta)}{\lambda}\right).$$

<div class="definition-grid"><div>$p_{0,k}$: target density at planning time $k$.<br>$Z_k$: normalizing integral.<br>$\mathbf1_\Theta$: indicator of the bounded parameter domain.</div><div>$v_k$: numerical acceptance indicator.<br>$\lambda>0$: MBD cost temperature.<br>$\eta$: optimistic fraction, separate from $\lambda$.</div></div>

A bounded domain and an accepted subset of positive volume with finite cost give a positive, finite normalizer.

<div class="key-line">The density and weighted mean are over policy parameters. Filtered inputs and executed states remain rollout outputs.</div>
<div class="source">Pan et al., MBD Sec. 4.1 supplies the generic target construction. The optimistic monitoring criterion is the proposed addition.</div>

## The ordinary MBD proposal remains the reference {#optimistic-reference-proposal data-section="4 · MBD optimization"}

Retain the forward-noise model from the preliminaries:

$$y_i=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_i}\,\theta+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_i}\,\epsilon,
\qquad \epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I),\qquad \bar\alpha_i=\prod_{j=1}^{i}\alpha_j.$$

At level $i$, its Gaussian proposal in clean parameter coordinates is

$$\phi_i(\theta)=\mathcal N\!\left(\theta;\frac{y_i}{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_i}},\sigma_i^2I\right),
\qquad \sigma_i^2=\bar\alpha_i^{-1}-1.$$

<div class="definition-grid"><div>$i=N,\ldots,1$: reverse diffusion level.<br>$y_i$: current noisy parameter vector.<br>$0<\alpha_i<1$: per-step variance retention.</div><div>$\bar\alpha_i$: cumulative variance retention.<br>$\phi_i$: ordinary Gaussian proposal density.<br>$\sigma_i^2$: variance per parameter coordinate.</div></div>

<div class="key-line">We adapt where evaluation samples are drawn. The forward diffusion model stays unchanged.</div>
<div class="source">Pan et al., Eqs. (3), (6), (8) and (9). The proposal here follows Eq. (8)'s indexing.</div>

## Evaluated policies identify promising alternatives {#optimistic-archive-priority data-section="4 · MBD optimization"}

Maintain $\mathcal A_k$, the archive of evaluated policy parameter vectors in the current planning call. Its accepted expected-cost incumbent is

$$\theta_{\mathrm{inc}}\in\underset{\theta\in\mathcal A_k:\,v_k(\theta)=1}{\arg\min}\ \widehat J_k(\theta).$$

For an accepted archive entry $\theta_a$, define the **optimism margin** and **sampling priority**:

$$b_k(\theta_a)=\widehat J_k(\theta_a)-J^{\mathrm{opt}}_{k,\eta}(\theta_a),$$
$$a_a=\left[J^{\mathrm{opt}}_{k,\eta}(\theta_{\mathrm{inc}})-J^{\mathrm{opt}}_{k,\eta}(\theta_a)\right]_+
\mathbf1\{b_k(\theta_a)>0\}.$$

<div class="definition-grid"><div>$a$: archive-entry index on this slide.<br>$b_k$: gap between mean and optimistic cost.<br>$a_a$: priority for additional sampling near that entry.</div><div>Positive priority requires a better optimistic cost than the incumbent and a positive optimism margin. Rejected entries are ineligible.</div></div>

<div class="small-note">These quantities describe cost variation and search priority. Neither estimates the benefit of a future observation.</div>

## An adapted proposal preserves ordinary sampling {#optimistic-mixture data-section="4 · MBD optimization"}

Normalize positive archive priorities, then place a Gaussian around each qualifying policy:

$$\nu_a=\frac{a_a}{\sum_ba_b},\qquad
\psi_i(\theta)=\sum_{a:a_a>0}\nu_a\,\mathcal N(\theta;\theta_a,\sigma_i^2I).$$

Mix this archive proposal with the ordinary Gaussian:

$$\boxed{q_i^{\mathrm{prop}}(\theta)=(1-\rho)\phi_i(\theta)+\rho\psi_i(\theta),\qquad 0<\rho<1}$$

<div class="definition-grid"><div>$\nu_a$: normalized sampling priority.<br>$\psi_i$: archive-centered mixture density.<br>$b$: summation index over archive entries.</div><div>$\rho$: fraction assigned to archive sampling.<br>$q_i^{\mathrm{prop}}$: sampling density, distinct from clarity $q$.<br>No positive priority: use $q_i^{\mathrm{prop}}=\phi_i$.</div></div>

<div class="key-line">The ordinary Gaussian remains available. Extra samples explore already discovered alternatives more closely.</div>
<div class="small-note">Freeze the proposal for a batch. Update the archive after evaluating that batch. Discovery of every route is not guaranteed.</div>

## Importance correction preserves the intended target {#optimistic-importance data-section="4 · MBD optimization"}

Draw $K$ fresh parameter vectors $\theta_n\sim q_i^{\mathrm{prop}}$, $n=1,\ldots,K$. Their unnormalized weights are

$$\widetilde w_n=\mathbf1_\Theta(\theta_n)v_k(\theta_n)
\exp\!\left(-\frac{J^{\mathrm{opt}}_{k,\eta}(\theta_n)}{\lambda}\right)
\frac{\phi_i(\theta_n)}{q_i^{\mathrm{prop}}(\theta_n)}.$$

$$w_n=\frac{\widetilde w_n}{\sum_{m=1}^{K}\widetilde w_m},\qquad
\bar\theta=\sum_{n=1}^{K}w_n\theta_n.$$

<div class="definition-grid"><div>$\widetilde w_n$: weight before normalization.<br>$w_n$: normalized importance weight.<br>$\bar\theta$: weighted parameter mean.</div><div>$\phi_i/q_i^{\mathrm{prop}}$ corrects for the changed sampling density.<br>$K$: number of fresh samples in the batch.<br>$m$: sample index in the denominator.</div></div>

<div class="key-line">The target changes the preference. The corrected proposal changes how efficiently that target is searched.</div>
<div class="small-note">Use the full mixture density in the denominator. Old archive entries guide sampling but are not appended as if drawn from this batch.</div>

::: {.notes}
Derivation: the conditional mean in MBD Eq. (9a) is integral theta*phi_i*p_0 divided by integral phi_i*p_0. Rewriting each integral as an expectation under q_i^prop introduces phi_i/q_i^prop. Self-normalization gives the displayed finite-sample estimate; it need not be unbiased at finite K. Since q_i^prop >= (1-rho)*phi_i, the density ratio is bounded above by 1/(1-rho). Do not use the density of only the mixture component that generated a sample. With importance correction, adapting a proposal alone does not introduce the optimistic preference into the target.
:::

## Score estimation and the next diffusion level {#optimistic-denoising data-section="4 · MBD optimization"}

Use the corrected parameter mean in the original MBD score and reverse update:

$$\widehat s_i=\frac{-y_i+\sqrt{\bar\alpha_i}\bar\theta}{1-\bar\alpha_i},\qquad
y_{i-1}=\frac{y_i+(1-\bar\alpha_i)\widehat s_i}{\sqrt{\alpha_i}}
=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{i-1}}\,\bar\theta.$$

<div class="definition-grid"><div>$\widehat s_i$: estimated gradient of the noisy target's log density.<br>$y_{i-1}$: noisy parameter vector for the next level.</div><div>$\bar\alpha_0=1$: clean endpoint.<br>The next ordinary proposal centers on $\bar\theta$ with its reduced noise variance.</div></div>

**If $i>1$:** construct the next mixture and draw a new batch.<br>
**If $i=1$:** diffusion ends and final policy reevaluation begins.

<div class="key-line">A weighted mean may describe a different, infeasible route. Evaluate the final vector before accepting it.</div>
<div class="small-note">Evaluate weights in log space. Outside $\Theta$: zero weight, without clipping. If all weights vanish, record failure and retry or retain an evaluated feasible policy.</div>

## Selection uses fresh performance fields {#optimistic-selection data-section="4 · Selection and real learning"}

After diffusion, collect the leading accepted archive policies, the expected-cost incumbent and the retained previous-plan continuation. Also evaluate the final diffusion vector before admitting it.

Reevaluate these policies with a **fresh, shared bank** of performance fields. Use the same execution filter and acceptance checks.

$$\theta_k^\star\in\underset{\theta\in\mathcal A_k^{\mathrm{val}}}{\arg\min}\
J^{\mathrm{opt,val}}_{k,\eta}(\theta).$$

<div class="definition-grid"><div>$\mathcal A_k^{\mathrm{val}}$: policies accepted on the fresh bank.<br>$J^{\mathrm{opt,val}}_{k,\eta}$: optimistic score recomputed on that bank.</div><div>The same new fields are shared across policies.<br>Keep the optimistic criterion for selection; changing to expected cost would alter the decision rule.</div></div>

<div class="small-note">This is a selection check, not an unbiased final test or a probabilistic safety certificate. If none passes, use the declared runtime fallback and record a planning failure.</div>

## Real measurements change the next planning call {#optimistic-real-learning data-section="4 · Selection and real learning"}

Execute the selected policy only for the next replanning interval $\Delta t>0$, using the actual execution filter.

Collect disturbance observations along the actual trajectory, then update POAM:

$$\mathcal B_{k+1}^d=\operatorname{POAMUpdate}(\mathcal B_k^d,\mathcal D_k^{d,\mathrm{real}}).$$

<div class="definition-grid"><div>$\mathcal D_k^{d,\mathrm{real}}$: real disturbance measurements and their locations collected during the interval.</div><div>$x_{k+1},q_{k+1}$: attained state and clarity.<br>The next planning call starts from these attained quantities.</div></div>

The updated posterior changes both the performance-field distribution and the filter construction at the next call.

<div class="key-line">Learning occurs through executed motion. The planning rollout contains no hypothetical posterior updates.</div>

## Why optimism could help a long mission {#optimistic-long-mission data-section="4 · Intended long-term behavior"}

An uncertain route can look worse on average yet offer favorable plausible monitoring. Optimism can make the robot try that route earlier.

| During the early visit | During later monitoring |
|---|---|
| Real motion exposes the robot to an uncertain disturbance region. | The updated spatial model changes later route and control decisions. |
| Travel or imperfect tracking may increase monitoring deficit. | Repeated useful visits may repay that early cost. |

The hypothesis needs a persistent disturbance pattern, informative measurements, usable spatial generalization and enough remaining mission time to exploit the information.

<div class="key-line">The full-mission deficit must show whether the later gain actually repays the early loss.</div>
<div class="small-note">The criterion does not predict observation informativeness or future belief changes. Optimism can also favor an alternative that teaches little or remains costly.</div>

## Early optimism needs an explicit schedule to fade {#optimism-schedule data-section="4 · Method assessment"}

The supplied method uses a specified $\eta$. By itself, this does not force optimism to decrease with physical time. Real learning may narrow the distribution of monitoring costs, but that effect is not guaranteed.

**Optional ablation for the early-optimism hypothesis:**

$$\eta(t)=\eta_0+(1-\eta_0)\min(t/T_{\mathrm{anneal}},1).$$

<div class="definition-grid"><div>$t$: elapsed physical mission time.<br>$\eta_0\in(0,1)$: initial optimistic fraction.</div><div>$T_{\mathrm{anneal}}>0$: time at which the criterion reaches the full mean, $\eta=1$.</div></div>

<div class="key-line">Compare a fixed fraction with a fraction that grows toward one. The schedule is a proposed ablation, not part of the supplied core method.</div>
<div class="small-note">No fraction, schedule, sample count or computational budget is selected here as an established optimum.</div>

## Comparison with MBD {.section-break #optimistic-mbd-comparison data-section="5 · Comparison with MBD"}

<div class="section-number">5</div>
<div class="section-subtitle">A different task target and a corrected sampling proposal.</div>
<div class="section-agenda">The forward diffusion and reverse score update retain their original form</div>

## Algorithm comparison with the MBD paper {#optimistic-algorithm-comparison data-section="5 · Comparison with MBD"}

<div class="algorithm-grid"><div><h3>Model-based diffusion</h3><ol><li>Define task cost and feasibility over the decision vector.</li><li>Initialize the noisy vector $y_N$.</li><li>At level $i$, draw decisions from $\phi_i$.</li><li>Evaluate cost and constraint factors through the model.</li><li>Normalize target-density weights and form the decision mean.</li><li>Estimate the score and update $y_i$ to $y_{i-1}$.</li></ol></div><div><h3>Proposed monitoring method</h3><ol><li>Define optimistic executed-monitoring cost and sampled acceptance over $\theta$.</li><li>Evaluate seeds and continuation; initialize $y_N$ and the policy archive.</li><li>At level $i$, draw policies from $q_i^{\mathrm{prop}}$.</li><li>Predict filtered motion and clarity in coherent performance fields.</li><li>Include $\phi_i/q_i^{\mathrm{prop}}$ in weights and average nominal parameters.</li><li>Apply the same score update. After diffusion, reevaluate and select.</li></ol></div></div>

<div class="source">Pan et al., Eqs. (6), (8), (9) and Algorithm 2. The adapted proposal and optimistic task criterion are proposed additions.</div>

::: {.notes}
This is an algorithm-level comparison. MBD is a generic model-evaluated optimization method and does not universally require a particular trajectory representation. Its trajectory-optimization instantiation uses rollout and constraint factors. Our nominal-policy representation is a specialization of the generic optimization variable. Initialization, finite budgets and numerical acceptance are separate choices. A warm start can be retained, but is not a new convergence result.
:::

## What changes and what remains {#optimistic-mbd-components data-section="5 · Comparison with MBD"}

| Component | Ordinary MBD | Proposed specialization |
|---|---|---|
| Decision | Task-dependent decision vector | Nominal policy parameters $\theta$ |
| Target objective | Model-evaluated task cost | Lower-tail executed monitoring cost |
| Rollout | Task-dependent dynamics and constraints | Disturbance, state-dependent filter and clarity |
| Sampling density | Gaussian $\phi_i$ | Mixture $q_i^{\mathrm{prop}}$ |
| Weight correction | Cancels for samples from $\phi_i$ | Explicit ratio $\phi_i/q_i^{\mathrm{prop}}$ |
| Forward noise and reverse update | Original MBD equations | Same equations |

<div class="key-line">Disturbance-aware task prediction is the foundation. Optimism changes the decision criterion; proposal adaptation changes the search.</div>
<div class="small-note">No additional convergence, safety or value-of-learning guarantee follows from this construction.</div>

## Planned evaluation {.section-break #optimistic-evaluation data-section="6 · Planned evaluation"}

<div class="section-number">6</div>
<div class="section-subtitle">The revised method awaits implementation and experimental evaluation.</div>
<div class="section-agenda">Requested baselines, diagnostic ablations and long-mission measurements</div>

## Baselines separate planning from runtime filtering {#optimistic-baselines data-section="6 · Planned evaluation"}

| Method | Planning prediction | Execution filter |
|---|---|---|
| **Proposed** | Disturbed, filtered monitoring; optimistic cost; adapted MBD proposal | Current-belief filter |
| **Wind-blind planning** | Nominal dynamics without the disturbance or filter response | No added constraint filter |
| **Wind-blind planning with safety filter** | Same nominal planning as wind-blind | Same current-belief filter as proposed |

All methods retain the same vehicle, actuator bounds, sensing model and low-level tracking law. The two blind planners ignore disturbance inside their planning objective.

<div class="key-line">Primary replay: proposed versus disturbance-blind planning. The filtered blind baseline remains in the quantitative evaluation.</div>
<div class="small-note">Baseline convention for review: runtime wind estimation and tracking compensation are shared; the unfiltered baseline differs by omitting the added constraint filter. Report collisions and failures without removing those runs.</div>

::: {.notes}
The baseline convention assigns wind-blind planning no added constraint filter and the second blind baseline the same runtime filter as proposed; both use the same wind-blind planning model. This convention must remain fixed across comparisons. Sharing estimation and tracking compensation isolates planning awareness from controller differences. Proposed versus filtered blind is the stronger control-matched planning contrast. The primary visualization compares proposed versus unfiltered disturbance-blind; all three appear in numerical tables. No new results are available.
:::

## Ablations separate optimism from sampling {#optimistic-ablations data-section="6 · Planned evaluation"}

| Ablation | Monitoring criterion | Parameter sampling | Question |
|---|---|---|---|
| Expected-cost disturbance-aware | Full mean, $\eta=1$ | Ordinary Gaussian | Does optimism help? |
| Optimistic disturbance-aware | Lower tail, fixed $\eta<1$ | Ordinary Gaussian | What does optimism alone do? |
| **Proposed** | Same lower tail | Corrected mixture | Does proposal adaptation help? |
| Fading optimism | $\eta(t)$ grows toward 1 | Corrected mixture | Is early optimism sufficient? |

Use the same runtime filter, real learning and policy representation across these four comparisons. Compare both equal rollout budgets and measured computation time.

<div class="small-note">Also vary the number of performance fields $S$, optimistic fraction $\eta$, mixture fraction $\rho$ and prediction horizon $T$. Two fields with $\eta=0.25$ reduce to the minimum of two costs.</div>

## Evidence needed for a long-term learning benefit {#optimistic-evidence-plan data-section="6 · Planned evaluation"}

Measure cumulative clarity deficit throughout the mission, per-region deficit, completed visits, tracking error, constraint failures and computation time.

**To explain the mechanism:** record the selected route, its sampled cost distribution, actual wind observations, posterior error and later changes in decisions.

**To test the learning explanation:** compare real posterior updates with a frozen-posterior diagnostic while holding the remaining algorithm fixed. A lower uncertainty estimate alone is insufficient evidence.

<div class="key-line">Use independent mission realizations and seeds, including failures. Report early cost, late cost and total cost.</div>
<div class="small-note">The fresh selection bank is part of the planner. Final evaluation requires separate disturbance realizations. Account for missed replanning deadlines instead of pausing physical time during planning.</div>

## Method assessment before implementation {#optimistic-assessment data-section="6 · Planned evaluation"}

**The specification is mathematically coherent:** a defined optimistic target, a state-dependent execution model and an importance-corrected proposal.

**The intended payoff is conditional:** an early experiment can improve later monitoring when its observations change useful future decisions. The optimistic criterion does not calculate that payoff.

**Important failure modes:** favorable-tail sampling error, poorly calibrated wind beliefs, repeated optimism about uninformative regions, inadequate route representation and excessive computation time.

<div class="key-line">The next stage is to test the hypothesis. Existing simulations provide no evidence for this revised algorithm.</div>
<div class="small-note">The former anticipated-learning method, its interactive explanations and its A/B results are preserved after the source slide in the archive.</div>
